newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn U-turn makes EMU task harder, Swedes opt out.
newsitem.headline: Bonn U-turn makes EMU task harder, Swedes opt out.

text.p: Germany's struggle to qualify for Europe's planned single currency grew harder still on Tuesday, but a likely member of France's new Socialist government pledged it would go ahead on time.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl, facing the deepest crisis in his record 14 years in office, backed down in a confrontation with the Bundesbank over government plans to revalue gold reserves.
Kohl had planned to use the windfall gain this year to help reduce state debt and make it easier to qualify for the single currency -- a scheme the central bank had described as cooking the books.

The humiliating climbdown creates another 10 billion mark ($5.8 billion) hole in Bonn's 1997 budget which the chancellor must desperately try to fill through privatisations, budget cuts or tax increases.
Sweden, one of the European Union's newest members, announced for its part that it would not join the new euro currency at the planned launch date in 1999 because the project was too shaky.

The German gold row and Sunday's shock election victory by the French left have thrown financial markets into frenzied speculation over prospects for Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).
The single currency, a historic project for the world's most powerful trading bloc, is unthinkable without the participation of Paris and Bonn.
While most analysts still expect it to happen, some fear a watering-down of the qualifying criteria for the euro, which include limits on inflation, budget deficits and public debt.
That would make it easier for countries like Spain and Italy to qualify, but could mean a weaker euro with diminished credibility.

Kohl was forced to yield after members of his own party sharply criticised the gold revaluation plan. Coalition sources said the windfall from it would now be transferred to Bonn only in 1998, a year too late to meet EU targets to qualify for the single currency.
Kohl has staked his enormous prestige on steering Europe's most powerful economy into monetary union, and to that end will seek a record fifth term of office next year.
"The situation is more serious and difficult than it has ever been during the whole life of this government," said Alois Glueck, a key ally of Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

In France, new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has made clear he will not impose further austerity to help France qualify for EMU. He will also depend for a parliamentary majority on Communists who are hostile to the single currency.
Asked about the planned euro launch date of January 1, 1999, Socialist European Affairs spokeswoman Elisabeth Guigou said: "Of course we must respect this deadline."

On the other hand, the Socialists have said they want to renegotiate the EU "stability pact" meant to penalise budget deficits after the launch of the euro and agreed in Dublin last year after lengthy negotiations.

Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson told a news conference the single currency project was too shaky and that public opinion in his country was solidly against. Events in both Germany and France had underlined the uncertainty.
"We are going to hold back on Swedish membership but we are not giving up our room for manoeuvre," Persson said.
"The question will be settled either through a normal election, a snap poll or through a referendum."

Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said any delay to the euro would be bad for Europe and for Italy. "The government has realised from the outset that it is in the interests of our country to take part in creating a single currency and that any suggestion of a postponement is against the interests of Europe and of Italy," he said in a statement.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi told a talk show on Monday night that any delay could prove fatal to the whole project.
